# Periprocedural management of oral anticoagulant therapy

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Preoperative and postoperative care > Periprocedural management of oral anticoagulant therapy*

[Original Article Link](/library/2r0Tgh)

---

## Summary

<u>Oral anticoagulants</u> include <u>vitamin K antagonists</u> (<u>VKAs</u>) and <u>direct oral anticoagulants</u> (<u>DOACs</u>). Periprocedural management of patients on long-term <u>oral anticoagulants</u> (e.g., for the prevention of <u>stroke</u> and systemic <u>thromboembolism</u>) is a field of ongoing research and there is currently no universal validated strategy. Management of <u>anticoagulants</u> in the periprocedural period should be tailored to the patient and the procedure in consultation with the proceduralist and anesthetist. Although invasive procedures performed on patients receiving <u>anticoagulants</u> are associated with an increased risk of bleeding, discontinuing <u>anticoagulants</u> increases the risk of <u>thrombosis</u>. Therefore, <u>anticoagulant</u> therapy should not be routinely interrupted periprocedurally, but instead, the decision should be based on the <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u> and the <u>periprocedural thrombotic risk</u>. Once interrupted, <u>VKAs</u> take time to achieve therapeutic anticoagulation on reinitiation, and hence, <u>bridging anticoagulation</u> with a short-acting <u>parenteral anticoagulant</u> is required in patients at high <u>thrombotic</u> risk. <u>Bridging anticoagulation</u> is not routinely required for patients on <u>DOACs</u>, as they have a short <u>half-life</u> and, if discontinued, can rapidly achieve therapeutic anticoagulation on reinitiation.

For urgent <u>reversal of anticoagulation</u> (e.g., for emergency procedures that cannot be delayed and/or for <u>major bleeding</u>), see “<u>Anticoagulant reversal</u>.”

---

## Periprocedural management of VKAs

### Approach [[3]](/library/vibAtt)




* Consult relevant specialists and follow institutional protocols if available.

* Assess the need to interrupt <u>VKAs</u> based on <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u>.

* If <u>VKAs</u> are to be interrupted:

* Determine the timing of <u>VKA interruption</u> based on preprocedural <u>INR</u> levels.

* Determine the need for <u>bridging anticoagulation</u> based on <u>periprocedural thrombotic risk</u>.

* Resume <u>VKAs</u> 12–24 hours after the procedure; consider delaying <u>VKA</u> resumption if <u>postprocedural bleeding risk</u> is high.





> [!TIP]
> The decision of whether to interrupt <u>VKAs</u> is based on <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u>. If <u>VKAs</u> are interrupted, the need for <u>bridging anticoagulation</u> is determined based on <u>periprocedural thrombotic risk</u>.




### VKA interruption [[2]](/library/vbdAvo0)[[3]](/library/vibAtt)[[6]](/library/z7crod0)




<u>VKA interruption</u> is the temporary discontinuation of <u>VKAs</u> before an elective invasive procedure to minimize <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u>.




* High <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u>: Interrupt <u>VKA</u>.

* Uncertain <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u>

* <u>Patient-related factors for periprocedural bleeding</u> present: Interrupt <u>VKA</u>

* No patient-related factors for bleeding: Consider interruption.

* Low <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u>: <u>VKAs</u> may be continued.

* <u>Patient-related factors for periprocedural bleeding</u> present: Consider interruption.

* No patient-related factors for bleeding: Do not interrupt <u>VKA</u>.

* Timing (if <u>VKA</u> is interrupted): Assess <u>INR</u> 5–7 days before the procedure.

* <u>INR</u> ≤ 3.5: Interrupt <u>VKA</u> 5 days before the procedure.

* <u>INR</u> > 3.5: Interrupt <u>VKA</u> ≥ 6 days before the procedure.





### Bridging anticoagulation [[3]](/library/vibAtt)




Periprocedural bridging anticoagulation involves the temporary administration of a short-acting <u>parenteral anticoagulant</u> after <u>VKA interruption</u> for an invasive procedure.




* High <u>periprocedural thrombotic risk</u>: <u>Bridging anticoagulation</u> is typically required.

* Low <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u>: Initiate preprocedural <u>bridging anticoagulation</u>.

* High <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u> (e.g., <u>ICH</u> within the past 3 months)

* Consider postprocedural <u>bridging anticoagulation</u>. [[3]](/library/vibAtt)

* If feasible, consider delaying the procedure in patients with a <u>thromboembolic event</u> in the past 3 months.

* Moderate <u>periprocedural thrombotic risk</u>

* Low periprocedural bleeding risk: Use clinical judgment; consult the proceduralist.

* High <u>periprocedural bleeding risk</u>

* Consider interrupting <u>VKA</u> without <u>bridging anticoagulation</u>.

* OR consider postprocedural <u>bridging anticoagulation</u>.

* Low <u>periprocedural thrombotic risk</u>: Do not bridge.





#### Preprocedural bridging anticoagulation [[3]](/library/vibAtt)




* Timing

* Initiate <u>bridging anticoagulation</u> when the patient's <u>INR</u> is in the subtherapeutic range.

* OR after 2–3 missed doses of <u>VKA</u>, if <u>INR</u> is not being monitored.

* Agents

* <u>LMWH</u>, e.g., <u>enoxaparin</u> DOSAGE: Administer the last dose 24 hours before the procedure.

* <u>UFH</u> DOSAGE : Administer the last dose 4–6 hours before the procedure. [[2]](/library/vbdAvo0)

* Nonheparin <u>anticoagulants</u>: indicated for patients with a history of <u>heparin-induced thrombocytopenia</u>

* Reassess <u>INR</u> 24 hours before the procedure.

* <u>INR</u> normal or subtherapeutic: Procedure can be performed.

* Persistently elevated <u>INR</u>: Consider delaying the procedure till the desired <u>INR</u> is achieved.





#### Postprocedural <u>bridging anticoagulation</u> and resumption of <u>VKA</u> [[2]](/library/vbdAvo0)[[3]](/library/vibAtt)




* All patients

* Ensure procedural site <u>hemostasis</u>.

* Assess postprocedural bleeding risk based on the following:

* Intraprocedural findings and adequacy of <u>hemostasis</u> (consult the proceduralist)

* <u>Patient-related factors for periprocedural bleeding</u>

* <u>Procedure-related bleeding risk</u>

* Low <u>postprocedural bleeding risk</u>: Resume <u>VKAs</u> 12–24 hours after the procedure.  [[2]](/library/vbdAvo0)[[3]](/library/vibAtt)

* High or uncertain <u>postprocedural bleeding risk</u>: Consider delaying <u>VKA</u> resumption. [[3]](/library/vibAtt)

* Additional measures in patients at moderate or high <u>periprocedural thrombotic risk</u>

* Consider overlapping <u>VKAs</u> with a <u>parenteral anticoagulant</u> (i.e., postprocedural bridging anticoagulation).

* Low <u>postprocedural bleeding risk</u>: Initiate <u>bridging anticoagulation</u> 24 hours after the procedure. [[3]](/library/vibAtt)

* High or uncertain <u>postprocedural bleeding risk</u>: Consider delaying <u>bridging anticoagulation</u> until 48–72 hours after the procedure. [[3]](/library/vibAtt)

* Agents and dosage: same as for <u>preprocedural bridging anticoagulation</u> [[3]](/library/vibAtt)

* Monitor <u>INR</u> closely.

* Discontinue the parenteral agent once <u>INR</u> is in the therapeutic range.
